author: harness:claude-code

patch.value: Scheduled auto-release has failed 32 of 84 times and nothing measures the rate, so a chronically degraded pipeline reads as healthy one run at a time

Measured 2026-07-27 from the workflow runs API. Across the full recorded history of event=schedule runs of auto-release.yml the conclusions are 52 success and 32 failure, a 38 percent failure rate, with failures on 2026-07-21, 2026-07-23 and 2026-07-24 inside the last week alone. Every control the project has is per-run: a failed scheduled run opens a blocker issue, closing that issue re-triggers the workflow, and the release-health reminder asks whether the most recent release tagged and published. None of these observes the rate. A pipeline that fails two days in three satisfies every existing check the day it succeeds, and the recovery path itself hides the signal, because the blocker issue is closed once the retry lands and the run history is the only remaining evidence. The gap is not a missing alert on a single failure; it is that reliability is not a tracked quantity, so no one can say whether the release automation is improving or degrading. The same 2026-07-27 window shows the sharper form of the problem: the daily release for the day was produced by two manual dispatches after a scheduled-path failure, and the still-pending scheduled run will find a release already cut and conclude skipped, which is indistinguishable in the run list from a healthy no-op.

Release automation reliability is expressed as a measured rate over a stated window, not as the conclusion of the latest run; A degradation in that rate is detectable without reading the raw run list, and the detection survives the blocker-issue recovery path closing its own evidence; A skipped run caused by the same-day guard is distinguishable in the reliability measure from a run that had nothing to release and from a run that failed; The measure names the failing stage, so a publish-step regression and a build-step regression are not aggregated into one opaque number
Make release-automation reliability a first-class tracked quantity with a trend rather than a per-run verdict
The project can tell whether its release path is getting better or worse, which is the precondition for spending effort on it deliberately
Three scheduled failures landed in the last seven days and the overall rate is 38 percent, yet every existing control reported healthy because each looked at one run
GitHub Actions hosted runners, unbraind/pm-cli, workflow auto-release.yml and its downstream release.yml publish job
Release automation reliability is observable as a rate with a threshold that fails when the pipeline degrades
32 of 84 scheduled runs failed and no artefact anywhere in the project records that fact or reacts to it

message: File the unmeasured release-automation failure rate found while verifying the daily auto-release

author: harness:claude-code

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Observation 2026-07-27 on the denominator used to compute the failure rate.

The Auto Release workflow has three triggers and they produce wildly different run volumes. The schedule fires once a day, which is the 84 runs this item measures. The workflow_dispatch fires on demand. The issues trigger fires on every issue closure in the repository, and because there is no concurrency key that collapses them, closing several issues at once produces a burst of near-simultaneous runs: four runs within one second at 12:09:44Z today, six at 08:45 on 2026-07-26, five at 08:54 today with one of them cancelled.

They are all correctly filtered at job level by the if condition that restricts issues-triggered runs to the bot-authored blocker recovery, so they skip in seconds and cannot cut a release. Two things still follow. The workflow run history is dominated by runs that were never going to do anything, which makes the pipeline look far busier and far healthier than the scheduled path actually is, and any rate computed over all runs rather than over event equals schedule will be wrong by an order of magnitude. And one of today's burst runs shows conclusion cancelled rather than skipped, which is the cancel-in-progress pattern that this project has already learned masks red gates elsewhere.

Neither changes the 32 of 84 scheduled figure this item owns, which was measured on the schedule event alone. Recording it so the denominator is not silently recomputed the easy way later.

value.text:
Rate re-measured live 2026-08-07 over the fourteen most recent scheduled runs: twelve success, two failure, so 85.7 percent on the trigger that carries the daily guarantee. The two failures are 2026-08-05, blocked by static-quality-gate, and 2026-08-07, blocked by sentry-telemetry-gate on "TypeError: Author acknowledgment target pm-iimv:1 is not an actionable unknown-author event" at candidate 36360b4b.

The second one is worth recording precisely because it is not a counterexample to pm-c3uru0's fix. That fix, which routes acknowledgment refusals through PmCliError with EXIT_CODE.USAGE, landed at 3bcacdee on 2026-08-07 07:49, and the failing scheduled run started at 04:36 against a candidate that predates it. The candidate was not red; the fix had simply not landed yet.

What the pair does show is the shape this item names. Both failures were repaired by a commit and then released by a manual workflow_dispatch, so the release record shows a successful cut on both days and the scheduled failure survives only in the run list. A reader reconstructing release health from tags, from npm dist-tags, or from the changelog sees fourteen consecutive daily releases. The rate is visible only by listing runs filtered to the schedule event, which is the measurement this item exists to institutionalize.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Rate measurement taken 2026-08-10, over the forty most recent scheduled runs of the daily Auto Release workflow, which span 2026-07-02 to 2026-08-10 inclusive with exactly one scheduled run per UTC day.

Eleven of forty failed. That is 27.5 percent, and it is a rate over a stated window rather than the conclusion of the latest run, which is what this item asks for. The failing days were 07-05, 07-10, 07-12, 07-15, 07-21, 07-23, 07-24, 08-05, 08-07, 08-08 and 08-10. The successful days number twenty-nine.

Two properties of the distribution matter more than the headline number. The failures are clustered, not uniform: 07-21 through 07-24 is three failures in four days, and 08-05 through 08-10 is four failures in six days, while 07-25 through 08-04 is eleven consecutive successes. A per-run alert cannot see a cluster, and a cluster is what distinguishes a chronically degraded pipeline from an unlucky day. And the recent cluster is worse than the older one, so the trend over the window is negative while every individual repair was completed and closed.

The measurement also confirms the mechanism this item already names. Every one of the eleven failures produced a blocker issue, and the blocker-issue recovery path closes its own evidence once a retry succeeds, so at any given moment the open-issue count is zero or one and carries no history of the rate. The count is recoverable only from the workflow run list, which no tracker surface reads.

One correction to how this rate should be computed, learned while taking it. Filtering the run list by workflow alone is wrong here, because the workflow also fires on the issues trigger and those runs burst several per second and mostly skip. The rate must be computed over the schedule event only, which is what the figures above do. A rate computed over all triggers would have reported a far larger denominator and a far smaller failure percentage, and would have been meaningless.

Finally, the fourth acceptance criterion on this item is now partly served by other work rather than by this one. The measure is required to name the failing stage. As of this session the failing gate records a structured document naming itself, its exit status and its verdict, so stage attribution has a source that does not require parsing run logs. That mechanism is pm-x63izf and it is the natural input to this item's per-stage breakdown.
